props.label: CLI gaps
props.title: Why each 'what really works' failure happens, and the fix

rows.gap: lev validator:validate --json puts JSON on stderr
rows.why: The handler is older than poly's handler contract: it reads its own --json flag, prints with console.log and returns nothing. In --json mode poly owns stdout, sends every handler print to stderr, then prints what the handler returned, which is nothing.
rows.fix: Handler returns the report object and prints nothing; poly renders it. (core/validator/src/handlers/validate.ts, core/poly/src/surfaces/cli/execute.ts:209-215)

rows.gap: lev validate / lev check refuse as ambiguous
rows.why: Three modules declare validate. Refusing is the rule you set on 09-28; `check` is advertised as an alias of a name that can never resolve.
rows.fix: Keep the refusal; drop the check alias.
Your 09-26 namespace ruling makes status a meta verb: one snapshot across modules, --deep for detail. That also covers what sitrep was for.

rows.why: Claims are only valid inside an exec worker; the help text predates that.
rows.fix: Fold claim submission into lev exec and delete the top-level verb.

rows.gap: lev exec loses a failing step's output
rows.why: The runner keeps only the exit code in the receipt.
rows.fix: Keep the failing step's output tail in the run artifacts and print it.

rows.why: The command never existed (core/build doctor hint).

rows.gap: lev workstream list flags a workstream invalid
rows.why: The /ws skill and the core/workstream schema disagree on the next-steps shape. Now it blocks writes too.
rows.fix: One owner picks the shape (ontology design), then fix data and the path join.

rows.gap: lev trace prints a log path that doesn't exist
rows.why: It prints the path whether or not the file was written.
rows.fix: Print it only when the file exists.

rows.gap: lev now prints an npm warning
rows.why: Launched through npm, which reads a pnpm-only project setting.

rows.gap: evaluator report cites a node that doesn't exist
rows.why: Enforcement provenance assumes a nodes-style flow.
rows.fix: Cite real node or step ids only.

items.title: Evaluators that check files: who opens the file?
items.insight:
**Example.** The proposal-readiness evaluator grades a proposal. One of its checks is that every file the proposal cites exists, for example `docs/specs/spec-exec.md`. Today the evaluator opens the disk itself to look.

Before any evaluator may block work as a gate, Lev tests it on known-good and known-bad samples inside a sealed box with no disk access, to prove it gives the right answer. An evaluator that opens the disk can't run in that box. So it can never be tested, and it can never become a gate.

Worse, if the AI step upstream says "that file exists", the evaluator believes the AI over the disk. That lets a missing file pass.

options.label: Code checks the files first and hands the evaluator the answers
options.why: e.g. the evaluator receives `spec-exec.md exists: yes`. It can be tested in the box, and the AI can no longer vouch for a file.

options.label: Let each evaluator read one declared folder, snapshotted for testing
options.desc: needs a new rule and a new name

options.label: Wait until evaluators run in their own process

props.content: 🧙🏽‍♂️ **[lev://mesh]** lev://recovery-orchestrator | ⚡ PAUSED · STAMPING ONTOLOGY + DNA | lev://design 📐

**Ontology design** (`.lev/pm/designs/design-fractal-source-framework.md`, part 1). A module declares two things in its own config.yaml. It declares **resolvers**: reserved folder names it owns, the way poly owns `handlers`. It also declares **entity kinds**. core/config finds every island once, checks that no two modules claim the same name, and hands each owner its matches. Entity kinds get list, show and resolve with no new TypeScript. Nesting like workstream, then task, then memory is one rule.

Today's ground truth:
- Folder patterns have three homes: 12 owner groups hard-coded in core/config, 8 modules that load their own sources, and a dead block in poly.
- Poly hard-codes `core/` and `plugins/`.
- Island support is implemented but declared nowhere.

Six older designs now point here as superseded.

**DNA design** (`.lev/pm/designs/design-dna-authoring-contract.md`). It counted where DNA lives today: 58 module contracts, 3 plugin-local DNA folders, 5 gate registries, and entity kinds split across three places. That adds up to 9 split brains. Its proposal is one home per kind of DNA per owner, and `plugins/dna` finds DNA files the same way poly finds handlers. It confirmed the lineage gate is hollow (its folder scan matches 0 folders).

The first build slice after your answers: the dna resolver declaration, plus the validator reading from the catalog, with no file moves.
